L06.objective: Predict how changing the mass of a balloon car affects the distance it travels. Test fairly, record the results and report the conclusion.

L46.objective: Use a model to locate the Solar System in the Milky Way and explain its relative size using a labelled inset.

L50.objective: Build a model from recyclable material, use stability and load tests to justify a design choice and explain why durability matters.

L01.materials: Clean shells, card, sponges, plastic caps, sorting trays
L01.induction: Display a smooth cap and a rough shell. Ask for properties pupils can observe directly.
L01.teach: Compare texture, shape and flexibility. Model sorting by one stated property and checking the rule against each item.
L01.practice: Observe four objects and record three features. Sort twice, changing the classification rule on the second attempt.
L01.assessment: Describe three observable features and classify two unfamiliar items using one rule.
L01.evidence: A shell may be hard, rough and curved. Use one stated rule, such as flexible or rigid, consistently for both items.
L01.closure: Ask why the same object can be grouped differently when the rule changes.

L02.materials: Rulers, three labelled objects, measurement grid
L02.induction: Show a ruler and ask where the object's end should meet the scale.
L02.teach: Model reading the scale at eye level, using zero or subtracting the start reading when necessary.
L02.practice: Measure three objects and record one consistent unit in a table. Compare one reading with a partner.
L02.assessment: Measure three labelled objects and submit a table with a column heading and units.
L02.evidence: The three rows match the object labels. Length is the difference between the end and start readings and uses a stated unit such as cm.
L02.closure: Ask what to do when the ruler's zero mark is damaged.

L03.materials: Three prepared sets of ramp observations, toy car, prediction slips
L03.induction: Show the same toy car stopping at different points on two surfaces.
L03.teach: Separate observation from inference. Use a measured contrast to propose friction as a possible explanation and to predict a repeat result.
L03.practice: Compare distances from repeated runs. Write a plausible explanation and predict a further run under unchanged conditions.
L03.assessment: A car travels 95, 100 and 98 cm on smooth card and 55, 52 and 58 cm on felt. Explain one possible cause and predict the longer run on repetition.
L03.evidence: The car may travel farther on smooth card because it experiences less rolling resistance. Previous results support that prediction but do not determine an exact distance.
L03.closure: Ask which sentence reports an observation and which offers an explanation.

L04.materials: Balloon-car snapshot cards, time labels, graph grids, rulers
L04.induction: Show two time-stamped pictures of the same moving car. Ask which one came first.
L04.teach: Model pairing position with elapsed time and plotting it. Compare intervals of equal duration on a distance-from-start graph.
L04.practice: Order snapshots, plot data and annotate changes in distance over time. Compare graphs with another group.
L04.assessment: Plot 0, 0.8, 1.3 and 1.3 m at 0, 1, 2 and 3 s. Identify the greatest gain and the interval with no change.
L04.evidence: The first interval gains 0.8 m, the second 0.5 m, and the last gains 0 m. A flat segment shows no change along the lane.
L04.closure: Ask how the graph would change if the car rolled back towards the start line.

L05.materials: Prepared balloon cars, floor marks, variable cards, measuring tape
L05.induction: Ask where the distance reading ends if a car rolls after the air escapes.
L05.teach: Define distance as start line to stopping mark in a straight lane. Model identifying changed, measured and controlled factors.
L05.practice: Draft a fair comparison for the same car with two securely attached loads. Label the start line, endpoint and control conditions.
L05.assessment: Define the distance measured, name the changed factor, and list two controls.
L05.evidence: Measure between the start line and the stopped car's reference mark. Added mass changes. Use the same car, inflation and floor surface.
L05.closure: Ask why a common stopping rule improves the comparison.

L06.materials: Matched balloon car and loads, tape measure, lane markers, report sheet
L06.induction: Show the same prepared car with and without an added load. Ask for a testable prediction.
L06.teach: Demonstrate repeated trials with the same inflation and lane. Check that the load remains secure and other factors are controlled.
L06.practice: Test two added masses, recording repeat distances. Compare results and write an evidence-based conclusion with the variables.
L06.assessment: Submit a hypothesis, results table and short report. State whether the data support the predicted difference and cite two readings.
L06.evidence: The hypothesis connects mass to distance. The table records both conditions with units, and the conclusion cites measured results. Report inconsistencies if present.
L06.closure: Ask which factor the class would control more closely on a repeat test.

R01.materials: Worked investigation card, results grid, correction slips
R01.induction: Show an investigation that changed both a car's load and its starting point. Ask what prevents a clear conclusion.
R01.teach: Model rewriting the hypothesis and identifying a confounded comparison. Show how to cite two results when interpreting a fair test.
R01.practice: Correct a sample plan, compare a fresh set of results and rewrite a conclusion to match the evidence.
R01.assessment: For a test of load versus distance, identify the responding variable and two controls. Rewrite a conclusion that claims one trial proves all future results.
R01.evidence: Distance is the responding variable. Same car and launch point are controls. A sound conclusion refers to the observed condition and evidence.
R01.closure: Ask what extra repeat would strengthen the conclusion.

L07.materials: Curriculum diagrams, six organ labels, function cards
L07.induction: Show the two curriculum diagrams and explain that the labels describe biological functions.
L07.teach: Teach organ locations and functions using standard terminology. Model matching an organ name, location and role on each diagram.
L07.practice: Label the six organs on blank diagrams, then match each label to a description using a partner check.
L07.assessment: Label testis, penis, vagina, ovary, Fallopian tube and uterus. Match each label with its biological function.
L07.evidence: Testes produce sperm, and the penis transfers sperm. The vagina receives sperm and forms the birth canal. An ovary releases an ovum, fertilisation usually occurs in a Fallopian tube, and the uterus supports development.
L07.closure: Ask pupils to distinguish where fertilisation usually occurs from where development takes place.

L08.materials: Fertilisation-to-birth sequence cards, labelled pathway diagram
L08.induction: Show an ovum and sperm diagram. Ask what forms when they join.
L08.teach: Place fertilisation in a Fallopian tube, then trace early development, implantation in the uterus and birth.
L08.practice: Arrange the four stage cards and draw an arrow between each stage. Label where the first two events occur.
L08.assessment: Sequence fertilisation, implantation, development in the uterus and birth. State where fertilisation usually happens.
L08.evidence: Fertilisation in the Fallopian tube precedes implantation in the uterus. Development continues in the uterus before birth.
L08.closure: Ask which organ supports the embryo and later the foetus.

L09.materials: Life-cycle images, labelled stage cards, diagram sheets
L09.induction: Ask pupils what happens to a population over time when individuals grow older and die.
L09.teach: Use a generational diagram to link births to population continuity. Distinguish an individual's growth from reproduction.
L09.practice: Draw a diagram across three generations and annotate the role of reproduction in continuing the population.
L09.assessment: Use the diagram to explain why human reproduction matters for the continuity of the population.
L09.evidence: Births add new individuals as earlier generations age and die. The visual identifies separate generations with a clear connection.
L09.closure: Ask pupils to point to the generation in which a new population member enters the diagram.

L10.materials: Nervous system outline, response cards, two-column chart
L10.induction: Describe hearing the school bell and deciding to pack up. Ask which part interprets the sound.
L10.teach: Map the central and peripheral divisions. Explain brain coordination and the spinal cord's role in conveying signals and coordinating some reflexes.
L10.practice: Label a body outline, pass signal cards through a path, and compare a voluntary response with a simple reflex example.
L10.assessment: Label brain and spinal cord and place nerves outside them in the correct division. State one function of each central structure.
L10.evidence: The brain processes information and coordinates responses. The spinal cord carries signals and coordinates some reflexes. Peripheral nerves are outside the brain and cord.
L10.closure: Ask which structure can coordinate a quick reflex before the person consciously reacts.

L11.materials: Signal arrows, hand-and-spinal-cord cards, response slips
L11.induction: Show a hand touching a cool object. Ask how the information reaches the central nervous system.
L11.teach: Model arrows from a sense receptor towards the central nervous system and from it to a muscle.
L11.practice: Trace a signal route and predict one possible effect if a pathway to either direction is interrupted.
L11.assessment: Trace a sensory and a motor signal for a hand movement. Predict one effect if the sensory pathway fails.
L11.evidence: A sensory nerve carries input towards the central nervous system. Motor pathways carry instructions towards muscles. The person may not sense the stimulus normally.
L11.closure: Ask which arrow carries a message towards the hand muscle.

L12.materials: Helmet and posture pictures, body outline, guide template
L12.induction: Show a helmet and ask what delicate structure it helps protect.
L12.teach: Connect each safe habit to a body structure and its function. Model an icon with a short reason.
L12.practice: Create an illustrated guide with three protective habits and sketch a nervous system signal route.
L12.assessment: Give two protective habits with reasons and mark how one stimulus is communicated in the body.
L12.evidence: A helmet helps protect the brain during cycling. Proper posture reduces strain from everyday tasks. A sensory signal travels towards the central nervous system.
L12.closure: Ask pupils how a picture and its caption together explain a habit.

R02.materials: Partial organ labels, reproduction stage cards, signal diagrams
R02.induction: Reveal one misplaced reproductive label and one reversed nerve arrow. Ask pupils to spot the errors.
R02.teach: Retell fertilisation through birth using a four-card sequence, then trace a simple sensory pathway.
R02.practice: Correct two diagrams, add a short explanation for each correction and verify both with a partner.
R02.assessment: Locate the ovary and uterus, state where fertilisation usually happens and fix a sensory arrow directed away from the spinal cord.
R02.evidence: The ovary releases an ovum; the uterus supports development. Fertilisation usually occurs in a Fallopian tube. A sensory signal travels towards the central nervous system.
R02.closure: Ask which correction shows a location and which shows a direction.

L13.materials: Labelled image cards, scale-bar examples, classifying grid
L13.induction: Show a micrograph with a scale bar and ask why the object appears large on screen.
L13.teach: Distinguish fungi, algae, protozoa, bacteria and viruses in the textbook classification. Note that viruses rely on host cells to multiply.
L13.practice: Sort supplied examples and compare what each image and caption can tell the observer.
L13.assessment: Match yeast, a unicellular alga, a protozoan, a bacterium and a virus image to their labels. Explain microscopic.
L13.evidence: The labels follow the supplied examples. Microscopic describes something too small for ordinary unaided viewing in this context.
L13.closure: Ask why a large image does not mean the organism is large.

L14.materials: Prepared micrographs and time-lapse clips, observation–inference grid
L14.induction: Show two images from a supplied sequence. Ask pupils to state what changed before interpreting it.
L14.teach: Introduce supplied records showing movement, a visible area change and gas from yeast activity. Distinguish an observation from its interpretation.
L14.practice: Compare three records and draw or write the visible evidence for movement, growth or gas production.
L14.assessment: Match each highlighted change to the process it supports and explain one limit of the evidence.
L14.evidence: Position change supports movement, expanding visible coverage supports growth, and gas production supports activity in the yeast example. These records do not establish the same behaviour in all types.
L14.closure: Ask what an image sequence shows that a single image cannot.

L15.materials: Prepared coded records, day-by-day images, blank graph, variable cards
L15.induction: Show two prepared observational records and ask what pupils would need to know before comparing them.
L15.teach: Model looking for a single changed condition and identical observation intervals. Compare matches and mismatches in supplied data.
L15.practice: Use coded records to identify variables, graph a reported indicator over time and compare observations with a prediction. Critique one confounded record.
L15.assessment: In a sample record, refrigerated A scores 0 and 1, while room-stored B scores 0 and 4 at Days 1 and 3 on the same visible-change scale. Identify the factor and explain the result.
L15.evidence: Storage temperature is the changed condition. Between Day 1 and Day 3, B shows a score increase of four and A of one. The conclusion applies to the supplied records.
L15.closure: Ask which conclusion the data support and which claim requires additional evidence.

L16.materials: Food and health case cards, two-column chart, captions
L16.induction: Show packaged yoghurt and a picture of spoiled food. Ask how related processes can have different effects.
L16.teach: Compare an intended food use such as yoghurt production with spoilage or illness, using cases rather than specimens.
L16.practice: Sort case cards, add how each effect arises and explain one match to a partner.
L16.assessment: Classify using bacteria to make yoghurt and microorganisms spoiling stored food. Explain the different outcomes.
L16.evidence: Selected bacteria help produce yoghurt under controlled production. Spoilage changes food quality and can make food unsafe.
L16.closure: Ask why a benefit depends on the context and type involved.

R03.materials: Prepared observation records, effect cards, evidence slips
R03.induction: Reveal a movement sequence and a food-use image. Ask what each can support as evidence.
R03.teach: Model pairing a claim with one feature of a supplied record or case card.
R03.practice: Match cases to helpful or harmful effects and choose one indicator from a time sequence to support a growth claim.
R03.assessment: Explain one helpful effect, one harmful effect and one piece of evidence from a prepared record.
R03.evidence: For example, yoghurt production is helpful and food spoilage is harmful. Increasing visible coverage supports growth in an image sequence.
R03.closure: Ask how the two observations differ from the interpretations.

L17.materials: Habitat scenarios, same-species and mixed-species cards, role charts
L17.induction: Show two birds using the same feeding area and ask what limited resource they might share.
L17.teach: Contrast prey–predator, competition and symbiosis. Model distinguishing competition within a species from competition across species.
L17.practice: Sort scenario cards and place likely contested resources beside competition examples. Stage one scenario and explain the classification.
L17.assessment: Classify a hawk hunting a rat, two stags competing for a mate, and two bird species competing for nesting sites.
L17.evidence: The hawk and rat illustrate predation, the stags illustrate intraspecies competition, and different bird species illustrate interspecies competition.
L17.closure: Ask which evidence in a scenario shows it is competition.

L18.materials: Symbiosis case cards, plus-zero-minus chart, arrows
L18.induction: Show a cattle egret feeding on insects disturbed by cattle. Ask who benefits in this example.
L18.teach: Model benefit, harm and no clear effect. Demonstrate using the two partners' outcomes to name the relationship.
L18.practice: Annotate three given pairs with the effect on each animal, then classify each relationship.
L18.assessment: Classify cleaner fish and its client fish, egret and cattle, and tick and dog using the case descriptions.
L18.evidence: Cleaner fish and client both benefit, egret benefits with little effect on cattle, and a tick benefits while harming its host.
L18.closure: Ask how a positive effect on one partner can still describe three different relationships.

L19.materials: Pre-grown comparison seedlings, photos, rulers, establishment records
L19.induction: Show dense and sparse sets of the same seedlings. Ask which other conditions need checking.
L19.teach: Set up or use pre-planted groups with the same seed type, medium, watering and light while varying spacing. Demonstrate measuring from soil level.
L19.practice: Measure selected seedlings and compare height plus leaf condition across groups. Note baseline conditions and report what crowding may change.
L19.assessment: Identify the spacing variable, one control, and an observed difference. Explain how competition could cause it.
L19.evidence: Spacing or density changes. A valid control is seed type or light. Record the measured difference and link crowding to competition for resources.
L19.closure: Ask why one seedling is weaker evidence than a comparison of several.

L20.materials: Photographs of an epiphyte and a parasitic plant, plant interaction maps
L20.induction: Show an orchid perched on a tree. Ask where it grows and whether it takes food from its host.
L20.teach: Compare competition, commensalism and parasitism among plants. Model connecting a plant relationship to an ecosystem observation.
L20.practice: Annotate an orchid–tree scene and a dodder–host scene. Add an effect on the relationship or habitat and explain it to peers.
L20.assessment: Explain how the orchid example differs from dodder on a host. Draw arrows or labels for the effects of both.
L20.evidence: The orchid gains support with little effect on the tree. Dodder draws resources from its host, which can be harmed.
L20.closure: Ask which observation would indicate resource loss by a host.

L21.materials: Extinction and threat case cards, timeline strips, classification mat
L21.induction: Show a dodo illustration and a Malayan tiger case card. Ask which represents a living species.
L21.teach: Distinguish extinction from extinction risk using verified or historical cases. Include one threatened plant card.
L21.practice: Place cases on an extinct versus at-risk mat and explain one difference in a caption.
L21.assessment: Classify the dodo, Malayan tiger and a threatened dipterocarp case from the class cards. Give a reason for each category.
L21.evidence: The dodo is extinct. The tiger and the example plant still exist but face documented risk. Use the case evidence rather than appearance.
L21.closure: Ask why low numbers and no surviving individuals are different claims.

L22.materials: Fictional habitat maps, pressure cards, cause–effect strips
L22.induction: Show maps before and after a road divides a forest. Ask what changed for animals.
L22.teach: Model evidence linking activities to population risk. Compare habitat destruction with illegal hunting or pollution in separate cases.
L22.practice: Trace a cause–effect chain and select a map or record detail that supports it.
L22.assessment: Explain one likely effect of forest fragmentation and give one distinct threat from the case cards.
L22.evidence: Fragmentation can cut access to mates or food. Hunting can directly remove animals from a population. Both claims link to their stated evidence.
L22.closure: Ask which detail directly supports each link in the explanation.

L23.materials: Protection measure cards, species pictures, proposal slips
L23.induction: Show an undisturbed reserve and a managed population recovery project. Ask what each tries to achieve.
L23.teach: Explain preservation as protecting existing natural conditions and conservation as managing or restoring populations and resources for continuity.
L23.practice: Classify proposed actions in context and propose a suitable measure for a named species. Explain where approaches overlap.
L23.assessment: Classify protecting an intact nesting beach and restoring a degraded nesting site. Explain how one action helps marine turtles.
L23.evidence: Protecting existing habitat exemplifies preservation. Restoring habitat exemplifies conservation. Either action can help provide suitable nesting conditions.
L23.closure: Ask pupils what would make a protection action appropriate for the chosen species.

L24.materials: Habitat case sheet, proposal cards, monitoring diagram, peer rubric
L24.induction: Present a threatened species map and ask where intervention would address the identified pressure.
L24.teach: Model evaluating one short-term and one long-term effect. Include a way to monitor whether the proposal helps.
L24.practice: Compare two actions, annotate predicted effects, and present a proposal informed by the stronger evidence.
L24.assessment: For a nesting beach, predict a likely result of limiting vehicle access and of restoring vegetation. Suggest one observation to monitor.
L24.evidence: Less traffic can reduce nest damage or disturbance. Appropriate vegetation restoration can protect habitat. Nest counts over time can help assess outcomes.
L24.closure: Ask which indicator the group would continue recording after the lesson.

R04.materials: Species case cards, risk labels, strategy cards
R04.induction: Show a forest clearing and ask what it removes from the habitat.
R04.teach: Review one example of an extinct animal and one action that protects a species still at risk.
R04.practice: Match three threats to suitable actions and choose one match to justify.
R04.assessment: Link habitat clearing to an appropriate protection strategy and explain the expected benefit.
R04.evidence: Protecting or restoring forest habitat retains shelter and food sources and can support survival of the species.
R04.closure: Ask which clue connects the threat to the strategy.

L25.materials: Toy cart, string, modelling clay, force arrows
L25.induction: Push a toy cart and pull the same cart with string. Ask pupils to show the direction of each action.
L25.teach: Demonstrate changes in shape, speed and direction, starting and stopping. Model placing arrows on the object acted on.
L25.practice: Work through cart and clay stations. Sketch three actions and the observed effect of each.
L25.assessment: Give examples of starting, stopping and changing shape by applying a push or pull. Add force arrows.
L25.evidence: A push can start or stop a cart depending on direction. A push can change the clay's shape. Arrows show the applied force.
L25.closure: Ask whether a force can change direction while an object keeps moving.

L26.materials: Identical blocks, smooth card, felt, spring scales, everyday-use cards
L26.induction: Slide a block on two surfaces and ask why it slows.
L26.teach: Model friction opposing relative motion. Use a steady pull and spring-scale readings to compare surfaces. Discuss one benefit and one drawback.
L26.practice: Repeat pulls with a matched block, log typical readings in N, then sort grip, wear and energy-loss scenarios.
L26.assessment: Use the measurements to compare the surfaces and explain one useful and one unwanted effect of friction.
L26.evidence: Greater force is needed to sustain the slide on the higher-friction surface. Friction can help shoes grip and can wear rubbing parts.
L26.closure: Ask how the fair comparison establishes a link with the surface.

L27.materials: Prepared block-and-scale stations, felt and card, two secured loads
L27.induction: Show two setups. Ask which isolates surface and which isolates load.
L27.teach: Demonstrate a steady horizontal pull. Keep contact surface and pull technique fixed while changing load, and use the same load when changing surface.
L27.practice: Rotate through two prepared comparisons. Record repeat readings at each station and compare within each pair.
L27.assessment: State the changed factor and one control for each comparison. Compare both sets of readings and report their trends.
L27.evidence: Change surface at constant load, then load at constant surface. A heavier load usually needs a greater steady pull on the same surface. Cite the measured differences.
L27.closure: Ask why the two investigations use separate comparisons.

L28.materials: Shoe sole pictures, slider samples, wheeled block, drawing cards
L28.induction: Show skidding footwear and a difficult-to-move box. Ask whether both need the same change.
L28.teach: Compare adding grip with reducing drag. Model selecting a surface or wheels and explaining the intended effect.
L28.practice: Sketch a design for an everyday friction problem and annotate where friction changes. Compare designs in pairs.
L28.assessment: Propose one change for a slippery shoe and one for a drawer that sticks. Explain why the desired effects differ.
L28.evidence: A grippy sole increases friction at the floor. A roller or suitable low-friction guide reduces resistance to drawer movement.
L28.closure: Ask where friction should stay high even if another part is designed to slide.

L29.materials: Clear plastic cup, water, firm card, tray, needle-free syringes
L29.induction: Show a sealed syringe containing air. Ask whether the air can push back.
L29.teach: Use a plastic cup and card above a tray. Compare with a small air gap and model air particles pushing on surfaces.
L29.practice: Observe the cup comparison and feel the push-back in a sealed syringe. Sketch arrows showing air pressure in each case.
L29.assessment: Describe what happens to the card in the demonstration and when air enters. Explain the role of outside air pressure.
L29.evidence: With a good seal the card stays briefly as outside air pushes upward. When air enters the cup the pressure difference is reduced and water can spill.
L29.closure: Ask how an unsealed setup helps test the explanation.

L30.materials: Altitude diagram, suction cup, picture of a drinking straw
L30.induction: Show a suction cup on a smooth tile and ask why it stays attached.
L30.teach: Compare pressure at the base and top of a mountain. Draw high-to-low pressure arrows for one device.
L30.practice: Annotate two altitude positions and one familiar device using the pressure arrows.
L30.assessment: Identify the higher-pressure altitude position and explain how a suction cup can be held against a tile.
L30.evidence: Pressure is usually higher at the mountain base. Lower pressure inside and higher outside air pressure help push the suction cup against the tile.
L30.closure: Ask what happens when air is let in beneath the cup.

R05.materials: Force arrows, surface scenarios, cup demonstration image
R05.induction: Show a toy cart, shoe and suction cup. Ask which example relies on friction.
R05.teach: Review force direction, opposing friction and the idea that air pushes on surfaces.
R05.practice: Match scenario cards to each concept and justify one from each column.
R05.assessment: Explain how a push moves a cart, why shoe tread helps, and why a closed suction cup sticks.
R05.evidence: A push can start a cart. Tread can increase grip. Outside air presses a well-sealed cup towards the surface.
R05.closure: Ask pupils to underline the evidence in each explanation.

L31.materials: Vehicle and animal cards, unit labels, classroom movement scenarios
L31.induction: Show a crawling insect and a highway speed sign. Ask why the same unit may be impractical for both.
L31.teach: Read cm/s, m/s and km/h as distance per unit time. Model selecting a unit that makes the scale easy to communicate.
L31.practice: Match example measurements to units, create new examples and peer-check the units against the context.
L31.assessment: Choose a convenient unit for a small toy car, a school sprint and a highway journey. Justify one choice.
L31.evidence: Examples are cm/s, m/s and km/h respectively. A sensible explanation matches the size of distances and times in the context.
L31.closure: Ask what the slash means in m/s.

L32.materials: Toy car, prepared ramp, tape measure, marked lanes, stopwatches
L32.induction: Show two cars at equal distance markers and ask which could get there sooner.
L32.teach: Model two comparisons: time for a fixed distance and distance in a fixed time. Keep the measuring method consistent.
L32.practice: Measure repeated runs using lane marks and timers. Compare both relationships and state an operational definition.
L32.assessment: Use two observations to describe how changing speed affects time or distance in the recorded trials.
L32.evidence: At a fixed distance, the faster car takes less time. In equal time it travels farther. Operationally, average speed is measured distance divided by elapsed time.
L32.closure: Ask which quantity must be fixed before saying less time means greater speed.

L33.materials: Distance–time cards, calculation slips, comparison tables
L33.induction: Ask how far a car travelling at 2 m/s would go in three seconds at constant speed.
L33.teach: Derive distance and time expressions from speed = distance ÷ time. Use compatible units in the worked examples.
L33.practice: Solve one example for each unknown, then write a short explanation comparing two journeys.
L33.assessment: Find the speed for 24 m in 6 s, distance at 3 m/s in 5 s, and time for 30 m at 5 m/s.
L33.evidence: The answers are 4 m/s, 15 m and 6 s. All three use compatible units and a correct relation.
L33.closure: Ask how the answer unit identifies the unknown.

L34.materials: Dated photo sequence, fictional food records, cause–evidence chart
L34.induction: Show photographs of the same food before and after visible changes. Ask which details changed.
L34.teach: Compare colour, texture and visible growth using supplied records. Explain how bacteria and fungi can cause spoilage.
L34.practice: Create an annotated photo comparison. Match one observed sign to an explanation and explain why appearance alone gives limited information.
L34.assessment: Name two visible indicators in the records and explain how microorganisms can cause spoilage.
L34.evidence: Examples include discolouration, texture changes and mould. Microorganisms can break down food and change its appearance or condition.
L34.closure: Ask whether food can look unchanged even when it is unsafe.

L35.materials: Food packaging pictures, preservation cards, matching chart
L35.induction: Show dried fruit beside a refrigerated product. Ask what each method changes.
L35.teach: Model linking low moisture, low temperature and acidity to slowed spoilage. Use ordinary food examples.
L35.practice: Match drying, refrigeration and pickling to their effects on the food environment.
L35.assessment: Explain the purpose of preserving food and why both drying and refrigeration can help.
L35.evidence: Preserving slows spoilage. Drying reduces available moisture, and refrigeration lowers temperature to slow many spoilage processes.
L35.closure: Ask why a refrigerated food can still spoil eventually.

L36.materials: Teacher-prepared food samples, sealed containers, balance, observation log
L36.induction: Show two prepared samples of the same fruit preserved in different ways. Ask what evidence can be compared.
L36.teach: Use a school-approved project with supervised drying and freezing of the same fruit. Demonstrate labelling and recording the sample condition.
L36.practice: Set up the two school-approved treatments, record baseline mass and appearance, then compare with teacher-provided dated follow-up records. Leave all samples for disposal.
L36.assessment: List both methods, one controlled starting condition and one difference in the resulting evidence.
L36.evidence: Begin with comparable portions of the same food. Drying typically reduces mass through moisture loss. Frozen samples are compared using their dated appearance and mass records.
L36.closure: Ask why a separate record is needed for changes that take several days.

L37.materials: Food labels, method cards, sequence strips, comparison table
L37.induction: Show plain frozen fish and dried packaged fish labels. Ask what methods the labels show.
L37.teach: Compare single methods with consecutive combined methods. Model a sequence chart for salted, dried and packaged fish.
L37.practice: Classify illustrative products and explain how different methods can address different conditions.
L37.assessment: Give two alternative methods for the same food, then describe an example that combines more than one in the same product.
L37.evidence: Fish can be frozen or dried. Salted dried fish combines salting and drying. Some products also use sealed packaging.
L37.closure: Ask pupils to distinguish a list of alternatives from a sequence of combined methods.

L38.materials: Seasonal fruit calendar, supply snapshots, response slips
L38.induction: Show plenty of fruit during harvest and little in the off-season.
L38.teach: Connect longer storage life with reducing waste and availability beyond harvest, using a labelled flow diagram.
L38.practice: Sequence harvest, preservation, storage and later use in a two-season scenario.
L38.assessment: Explain two reasons preservation can help a school canteen during and after a fruit harvest.
L38.evidence: Some surplus can be kept for later use, reducing waste at harvest and improving availability out of season.
L38.closure: Ask which benefit relates most directly to off-season supply.

R06.materials: Food method cards, storage scenarios, reasoning slips
R06.induction: Show a picture of a food and ask pupils to name one possible preservation method.
R06.teach: Review the purpose of slowing spoilage and one link between a method and a condition.
R06.practice: Match foods to methods and explain when a single or combined method fits.
R06.assessment: Recommend one method for surplus fruit and explain the condition it changes.
R06.evidence: Drying is one option. Reducing available moisture slows many spoilage processes. Other appropriate methods are accepted with a valid reason.
R06.closure: Ask pupils to link their answer to a condition rather than only a method name.

L39.materials: Clean picture cards for food, paper, plastic, glass and batteries, sorting mat
L39.induction: Show a banana peel and a plastic lid. Ask what could happen to each over time.
L39.teach: Distinguish sorting by material from sorting by biodegradability. Discuss when a waste item needs a separate collection route.
L39.practice: Sort the cards by type, then classify them by whether microorganisms can break them down under suitable conditions.
L39.assessment: Classify a banana peel, plain paper, a plastic lid and a glass jar. Define biodegradable using one of the examples.
L39.evidence: Banana peel and plain paper can biodegrade. Conventional plastic and glass are not readily biodegradable. Microorganisms can break down biodegradable waste under suitable conditions.
L39.closure: Ask why a glass item may be recyclable even though it is not biodegradable.

L40.materials: Clean waste cards, reuse and recovery choices, reason slips
L40.induction: Show a clean plastic container and vegetable trimmings. Ask how each could be used appropriately.
L40.teach: Compare reuse and recovery with disposal. Model linking a choice to the material and intended use.
L40.practice: Match four clean waste examples to a use or recovery route, explaining why the materials suit that route.
L40.assessment: Justify a useful route for vegetable trimmings and an intact plastic container.
L40.evidence: Suitable trimmings can go into an approved composting stream. A clean intact container can be reused for a compatible purpose.
L40.closure: Ask why damaged or unsafe items may need a different route.

L41.materials: Fictional class waste counts, 5R action cards, planning chart
L41.induction: Show a tally of single-use packaging from one day. Ask which number the class could reduce.
L41.teach: Model choosing a 5R action and comparing counts gathered over equal periods.
L41.practice: Plan one change, assign tracking responsibilities, and present a baseline and proposed follow-up measure.
L41.assessment: Propose one action and an indicator that can tell whether it reduced waste.
L41.evidence: For example, replace disposable drink cups with reusable ones and compare the count of discarded cups over two equal school periods.
L41.closure: Ask how comparing equal time windows makes the evidence easier to interpret.

L42.materials: Lamp, Earth and Moon balls, screen, shadow sketch sheet
L42.induction: Show three models and ask which must be in the middle for a lunar eclipse.
L42.teach: Keep the lamp fixed. Put Earth between the light and the Moon to model the Moon entering Earth's shadow.
L42.practice: Model the three-body order, then trace Earth's shadow and sketch where the Moon passes through it.
L42.assessment: Draw and label the lunar-eclipse alignment, including the shadowed object and the full-Moon phase.
L42.evidence: Sun–Earth–Moon. The Moon enters Earth's shadow. A lunar eclipse can occur at full Moon when the alignment is close enough.
L42.closure: Ask why being at full Moon alone does not guarantee an eclipse.

L43.materials: Fixed lamp, small Moon ball, Earth globe and screen, ray rulers
L43.induction: Show a small ball casting a patch of shadow on a larger model. Ask which body blocks the light.
L43.teach: Use indoor models to place the Moon between Sun and Earth. Trace light rays at the edge of the Moon model and compare the resulting shadow with Lesson 42.
L43.practice: Move the Moon model, locate the shadow on Earth and add straight rays to both eclipse sketches.
L43.assessment: Draw Sun–Moon–Earth and show why only some locations are in the Moon's shadow. Contrast with the lunar alignment.
L43.evidence: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks direct light along a narrow part of Earth's surface. In a lunar eclipse Earth blocks sunlight reaching the Moon.
L43.closure: Ask where partial shadow is represented on the globe.

L44.materials: Comparison diagrams, observer location cards, light-level picture cards
L44.induction: Show a small shadow patch on a globe and ask who can observe it from the surface.
L44.teach: Compare a location under the Moon's shadow with a night-side observer watching the Moon in Earth's shadow.
L44.practice: Annotate where observers are located and describe what changes in their view for each eclipse.
L44.assessment: Predict what an observer might notice during a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse. Explain which dip in brightness is local.
L44.evidence: A location under the Moon's shadow experiences reduced daylight. During a lunar eclipse an observer on Earth's night side may see the Moon darken or turn reddish.
L44.closure: Ask which event can darken a small area on the daytime side of Earth.

R07.materials: Eclipse alignments, straight-ray cards, correction slips
R07.induction: Reveal a diagram labelled lunar eclipse with the Moon in the middle. Ask pupils to verify it.
R07.teach: Review which body casts the shadow and use straight lines to show where its light is blocked.
R07.practice: Correct two mixed-up eclipse diagrams and label the location of each shadow.
R07.assessment: Give the three-body order and shadowed object for each eclipse.
R07.evidence: Lunar is Sun–Earth–Moon with the Moon in Earth's shadow. Solar is Sun–Moon–Earth with the Moon's shadow falling on part of Earth.
R07.closure: Ask which alignment puts Earth in the middle.

L45.materials: Galaxy images from a school-approved source, shape cards, comparison grid
L45.induction: Show a star field and a galaxy image. Ask how the two views differ in scale and content.
L45.teach: Explain galaxies as systems containing stars, gas and dust. Compare representative spiral, elliptical and irregular images and locate the Milky Way example.
L45.practice: Sort sample images by observed shape. Annotate a Milky Way image and compare it with two other examples.
L45.assessment: Define a galaxy, identify the Milky Way as a barred spiral and support two other classifications with visible features.
L45.evidence: A galaxy contains many stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Elliptical galaxies look rounded and irregular galaxies lack a clear regular shape in the sample images.
L45.closure: Ask why a photograph of a galaxy is different from a map of our Solar System.

L46.materials: Milky Way schematic, Solar System inset, coarse scale cards
L46.induction: Show a tiny dot on a galaxy sketch and ask what can fit within that marker.
L46.teach: Model using an inset and distinguishing a location marker from a drawing at true scale. Place the Solar System away from the centre in the Milky Way disc.
L46.practice: Create a main galaxy diagram and a magnified Solar System inset. Explain the relative scale during a gallery walk.
L46.assessment: Locate the Solar System in the Milky Way and explain why an inset is used to depict it.
L46.evidence: The Solar System is within the Milky Way disc. It is tiny relative to the galaxy, so showing its internal structure requires magnification.
L46.closure: Ask which label tells readers that the inset uses a different scale.

L47.materials: Card towers, simple paper beams, light counters
L47.induction: Push each tower lightly and then apply a small load to a supported beam. Ask how the tests differ.
L47.teach: Model stability as resisting tipping and strength as resisting failure under force. Apply each test separately.
L47.practice: Compare results for two simple models and label whether each observation is about stability or strength.
L47.assessment: Explain the difference using a tower that tips easily and a beam that supports several counters.
L47.evidence: Stability concerns tipping or staying upright. Strength concerns supporting force or load without failing. The two results measure different properties.
L47.closure: Ask if a strong model can still tip over easily.

L48.materials: Low card structures, tilt board, angle markers, recording grid
L48.induction: Show two models of the same height with different bases. Ask which may tip first.
L48.teach: Set up separate base-area and height comparisons. Model tilting slowly and recording the angle at first tip.
L48.practice: Run both comparisons with prepared light models. Repeat each trial and explain the observed effect of the changed factor.
L48.assessment: Name the altered and controlled factors in both comparisons. Decide which model was more stable from the angle readings.
L48.evidence: A wider base or lower centre of gravity typically requires a larger tilt before tipping. Base area and height are changed in different trials.
L48.closure: Ask why comparing larger base and shorter height at once cannot separate their effects.

L49.materials: Paper beam blanks, equal supports, light counters, load chart
L49.induction: Show a flat strip and a folded strip made from the same paper.
L49.teach: Model changing beam shape while holding paper, support span and load position constant. Repeat with equal geometry and different card materials.
L49.practice: Compare flat and folded beams plus the material pair. Add light counters centrally and record the load before marked bending or collapse.
L49.assessment: Use two tables to compare shape and material. Name the controlled factors and explain one outcome.
L49.evidence: Support span and load position stay fixed. Shape is changed in one comparison, material in the other. Evidence cites the observed maximum loads.
L49.closure: Ask which beam data compare strength rather than stability.

L50.materials: Pre-cut clean recycled card, tape, light counters, low push board
L50.induction: Show the material kit and explain the push and load tests pupils will use.
L50.teach: Model a quick assembly with two supports and a braced base. Explain that durability can reduce replacement.
L50.practice: Assemble a small model from prepared parts. Test for tipping and load, then annotate one design choice with an observed result.
L50.assessment: Show one change that improves stability or strength, and explain the benefit of a durable structure.
L50.evidence: A wider base can resist tipping, and a folded support can carry more load. Cite a classroom test result and link durability to less repair or waste.
L50.closure: Ask which evidence supports keeping a particular feature.

R08.materials: Short model test records, card structure sketches, fix cards
R08.induction: Show a model that tips easily and one with a bending beam. Ask if the failures have the same cause.
R08.teach: Review testing stability with a small tilt and strength with a recorded load.
R08.practice: Match failures to possible improvements and use the test records to justify the connection.
R08.assessment: For a narrow model that tips and a flat beam that bends, suggest separate improvements and predict what each test would show.
R08.evidence: A wider base can increase the tilt needed for tipping. Folding or bracing a beam may increase the load it supports.
R08.closure: Ask which change should be judged using a load rather than a tilt.

L51.materials: Tool timelines, field cards, archive pictures, investigation sheets
L51.induction: Show a hand tool and a modern counterpart. Ask what task both accomplish.
L51.teach: Model how scientific knowledge becomes a tool that addresses a limitation. Compare changes in communication, agriculture and transport.
L51.practice: Build a three-stage timeline for one field, then compare its development with another field in a gallery walk.
L51.assessment: Define technology and use two tool examples to explain which human limitation each addresses.
L51.evidence: Technology applies scientific knowledge to overcome practical limitations. A telescope extends distant viewing, and modern communication tools transmit messages over long distances.
L51.closure: Ask how a new feature changes what humans can do.

L52.materials: Technology case cards, benefit–drawback chart, decision slips
L52.induction: Show navigation on a phone and ask for one benefit and one cost.
L52.teach: Model weighing a trade-off in a concrete situation. Ask what responsible action addresses the drawback.
L52.practice: Complete a comparison using one case and present a use choice with a reason.
L52.assessment: Explain a benefit and a drawback of a navigation app, then give a responsible choice.
L52.evidence: Navigation helps find routes. Sharing location can reduce privacy. Use location only when needed or limit unnecessary access.
L52.closure: Ask how the chosen action addresses the drawback while preserving the benefit.

R09.materials: Technology cards, choice matrix, response strips
R09.induction: Show an online communication example and ask whose task it changes.
R09.teach: Review matching benefits, costs and actions using one worked case.
R09.practice: Select a familiar technology, compare effects and present one reasoned choice to a group.
R09.assessment: Give a benefit and a drawback of video calls and suggest one responsible practice.
R09.evidence: Video calls allow distant meetings but require equipment and connectivity. Protect meeting access or use a suitable alternative when access is limited.
R09.closure: Ask which evidence would help judge the choice in a real situation.

L04: Present a second time series from a car that stops sooner. Check axes and scaling before comparing the two runs.
Plot a second run on the same axes. Explain which interval has the greatest distance change in each run.
L07: Provide silent label checks and a card set showing the path of an ovum. Clarify terms using the two diagrams.
Trace the ovum from an ovary towards a Fallopian tube and identify which organ supports development. Review all six functions.
L10: Use a second scenario involving awareness of touch and contrast it with the reflex example.
Build both signal paths with arrows and label central and peripheral structures on each path.
R02: Provide two corrected examples with one label hidden in each. Model how to give a reason for a correction.
Rebuild both sequences from partial cues and explain one corrected relationship to a partner before the individual task.
L15: Reveal a confounded record and a second pair with repeated readings. Ask which comparisons are defensible.
Check the observation key, plot the new results and note where confounding or limited repetition weakens the claim.
L17: Assign groups a common resource and vary its availability in the scenario.
Compare scenarios with scarce and abundant resources, then explain when competition is expected.
L20: Introduce a crowded seedling group as a third case and ask how it differs from both symbioses.
Make a comparison chart showing resource competition, support and resource loss in the three plant cases.
L24: Provide a second location or pressure card to test whether the preferred proposal still fits.
Revise the proposal for the new scenario and justify which evidence changed the choice.
L26: Offer a second set of surface samples and a new real-life trade-off. Check repeatability at each station.
Compare repeated readings and choose a material where greater grip matters. Explain what an unusually high reading could mean.
L29: Run a second comparison with air in a sealed syringe. Model how the two demonstrations support the same general idea.
Sketch and compare how the syringe pushes back and how air holds the card. Mark which observation supports each explanation.
L31: Give speed cards containing mixed units and everyday contexts. Model reading one numerical speed aloud.
Write a contextual example for each unit and explain why comparing the numerical values alone could mislead.
L34: Add a case with incomplete visual evidence and ask what can reasonably be concluded.
Annotate limits of the available evidence and explain why the records cannot establish that a food is safe.
L37: Provide two different labels for the same kind of food. Ask pupils to read the processing information.
Build a method diagram showing alternatives for one product and a sequence for the combined product.
L39: Show a recycling symbol and a compostable-label example. Discuss why the sorting criteria answer different questions.
Reclassify the material cards and annotate which can be reused, recycled or sent to an approved organics stream.
L43: Vary the observer position relative to the model shadow and model partial versus deeper shadow.
Predict the view at three globe locations and revise the shadow sketch after checking the model.
L45: Show two different views of a spiral structure. Discuss how position and viewing direction change the image.
Make a labelled Milky Way schematic, then compare features with another galaxy and annotate limits of the images.
L49: Ask teams to exchange recorded tables and check test conditions before comparing outcomes.
Use a second group’s data to check consistency and suggest one improvement to control the load position or span.
L51: Assign two fields for comparison and model checking a date, purpose and new feature on each timeline.
Present timelines in groups and explain how two different tools extend a capability such as reach, speed or observation.
